content: Forecasting refers to the process of estimating outcomes in situations where the future is uncertain. Prediction is a related but broader term, often used to describe the estimation of outcomes based on time series, cross-sectional, or longitudinal data. In recent years, forecasting has evolved into a critical component of demand planning, particularly in the context of business operations for manufacturing companies. Demand planning, sometimes referred to as supply chain forecasting, integrates both statistical forecasting techniques and consensus-based processes. Forecasting is frequently discussed in the context of time-series data. Categories of Forecasting Methods Time Series Methods Time series methods rely on historical data to estimate future outcomes. These methods include: Moving average Exponential smoothing Extrapolation Linear prediction Trend estimation Growth curve analysis Causal/Econometric Methods Causal or econometric forecasting methods operate on the assumption that it is possible to identify underlying factors that influence the variable being forecasted. For instance, umbrella sales may be influenced by weather conditions. If the causal factors are well understood, projections of these influencing variables can be made and incorporated into the forecast. Examples of these methods include: Regression analysis (using linear or non-linear regression) Autoregressive moving average (ARMA) Autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) Econometric modeling Judgmental Methods Judgmental forecasting methods incorporate intuitive judgments, expert opinions, and probability estimates. These methods include: Composite forecasts Surveys Delphi method Scenario building Technology forecasting Forecasting by analogy Other Methods Other forecasting techniques include: Simulation Prediction markets Probabilistic forecasting and ensemble forecasting Forecasting Accuracy Forecasting accuracy is assessed by measuring the forecast error, which is the difference between the actual value and the forecasted value for a given period. Mathematically, this is expressed as: [ E_t = Y_t F_t ] Where: (E_t) is the forecast error at time (t), (Y_t) is the actual value at time (t), (F_t) is the forecasted value at time (t). Measures of aggregate error are often used to evaluate forecasting performance. In industry practice, business forecasters and demand planners frequently refer to the Percentage Mean Absolute Deviation (PMAD) as the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), although they typically compute this as a volume-weighted MAPE.
